name_arabic: جَابِرُ بْنُ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ حَرَام
tribe: Banu Salama of al-Khazraj — Ansar of Madinah
era: The Orphan of Uhud Who Taught Madinah
teaser: He lifted the cloth from his father's face at Uhud and kissed it. Nobody stopped him.

layers.title: Who
layers.subtitle: Son of one of the twelve, brother to many sisters
layers.content:
Jabir ibn Abdullah ibn Amr ibn Haram, of the Banu Salama, a clan of al-Khazraj. His mother was Unaysa bint Anama. His father's kunyah was Abu Jabir — the boy's name and the father's title were the same word, which tells you something about how that household saw itself.

Abdullah ibn Amr was not a follower. Ibn Sa'd records him among the seventy Ansar at the second 'Aqaba and, more than that, among the twelve leaders chosen from them. Jabir himself was there at 'Aqaba too, young, standing in his father's shadow on the night the Ansar staked the safety of every house they owned.

The description of the father survives, and it is not heroic in the way a listener expects: a bald, reddish man who was not tall. His closest friend, Amr ibn al-Jamuh, was tall. The two of them are inseparable in the records for a reason you will find in the fourth layer.

And there were the girls. Abdullah's household was full of daughters, and the last instruction he left, the night before Uhud, was about them: treat the daughters of Abdullah well.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley — entry on Abdullah ibn Amr ibn Haram: lineage, kunyah, presence at 'Aqaba among the twelve leaders, Jabir's presence at 'Aqaba, the physical description, and the instruction about the daughters narrated from Jabir through Abu Nadra

layers.title: The Conversion
layers.subtitle: A pledge in the dark, then years held back
layers.content:
Islam came to Banu Salama the way it came to most of the Ansar: through the pledge at 'Aqaba, taken at night, by men who understood they were committing their whole clan to a war they had not started. Jabir's father was one of the twelve who guaranteed it. Jabir stood among the seventy as a boy.

Then came the strange cost. His father would not let him fight.

Jabir was plain about it later. He said he went on nineteen expeditions with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and that he was at neither Badr nor Uhud, because his father held him back. Not from cowardice on anyone's part. Because there were girls in the house and somebody had to be alive in it.

So the first years of his Islam looked like nothing at all. The pledge, and then staying home while the two decisive battles of the community were fought without him. Everything he is known for — the hajj, the rulings, the thousands of narrations — sits on top of a young man who was told he was needed for something less visible and accepted it.

After Uhud he was never absent from a campaign again.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih Muslim, Book of Jihad and Expeditions, narrated by Jabir ibn Abdullah — nineteen expeditions, and his absence from Badr and Uhud
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, for 'Aqaba and the twelve leaders; Sahih Muslim, Book of Jihad and Expeditions, narrated by Jabir, for the nineteen expeditions and his father keeping him back

layers.title: With the Prophet ﷺ
layers.subtitle: A slow camel, a debt, and a marriage
layers.content:
What the sources preserve about Jabir beside the Prophet ﷺ is almost entirely domestic, and that is the point.

He was riding home from a campaign on a camel that had given up under him. The Prophet ﷺ caught up with him and asked why he was so far back, then bought the animal from him. When they reached Madinah he handed Jabir the price and the camel both.

On the same road he was asked whether he had married. Yes. A virgin or a woman who had been married before. A woman who had been married before. And Jabir explained himself without being asked: his father had been killed and left daughters, and he did not want to bring home a girl their own age. He wanted someone who could comb their hair and manage them.

And there was the debt. His father died owing more than the date-palms could yield in two years, and Jabir was being pressed. He asked the Prophet ﷺ to come with him so the creditors would not be excessive. The Prophet ﷺ walked around one of the threshing floors of dates, made supplication, sat down, and called the creditors in. They were paid in full, and what was left was the same amount again.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Marriage, narrated by Jabir ibn Abdullah — the camel and the question about his marriage
layers.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Marriage and Book of Sales, narrated by Jabir; the threshing floor and the discharge of his father's debt narrated from Jabir through Amir ash-Sha'bi in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III

layers.title: The Trial
layers.subtitle: The first man killed at Uhud was his father
layers.content:
Abdullah ibn Amr ibn Haram was the first Muslim killed at Uhud, in the thirty-second month after the Hijrah. The Prophet ﷺ prayed over him before the rout began.

Jabir came to the body where it lay shrouded, pulled the cloth back from his father's face, and wept, and kissed it. The Companions around him began to stop him. The Prophet ﷺ did not. He said instead: weep for him or do not weep — the angels went on shading him with their wings until they raised him up.

Jabir's mother had already tried to take him home. She loaded her husband and her brother onto a camel and brought them towards Madinah, and the Prophet's ﷺ caller went out: bury the dead where they fell. They were carried back.

And there was the burial itself. The Prophet ﷺ ordered that Abdullah ibn Amr and Amr ibn al-Jamuh be put in one grave, and gave the reason out loud: bury these two who loved one another in this world in one grave.

Tirmidhi records that the Prophet ﷺ told Jabir Allah had met his father and said, ask Me and I will give you, and that his father asked to be sent back to be killed a second time — and that «وَلَا تَحْسَبَنَّ الَّذِينَ قُتِلُوا فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ أَمْوَاتًا» was revealed about them.
layers.hadith_ref: Jami' at-Tirmidhi, Book of Tafsir, narrated by Jabir ibn Abdullah — what was said to his father
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley — Abdullah ibn Amr as the first killed at Uhud, the uncovering of the face narrated from Jabir through Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir and Abu az-Zubayr, the mother's camel narrated through Nubayh al-Anazi, and the single grave reported from Malik ibn Anas; Jami' at-Tirmidhi, Book of Tafsir, for the report on Surah Ali 'Imran 3:169

layers.title: The Legacy
layers.subtitle: Forty-six years later they opened the grave
layers.content:
Flood-water cut into the graves by the river bed and unearthed the two friends. Jabir went and looked. He said: I saw my father in his grave as if he were asleep — he had not changed at all. He was asked about the shrouds. The mantle was as it had been and the rue on his feet was still preserved. Forty-six years.

He had also, six months after the burial, taken the other man out of his father's grave and buried him alone, because he could not rest until it was done. Grief keeps working on people for decades.

He lived a very long time and spent it teaching in Madinah, blind at the end. If you have ever been taught how the Prophet ﷺ performed hajj — the order of it, the words, the stops, the sacrifice — you have been taught from Jabir. Muslim preserved his account of the Farewell Hajj at full length, and it remains the spine of the rites.

Al-Bukhari, in his chapter on travelling in search of knowledge, notes that Jabir rode a month to Abdullah ibn Unays in Syria for one hadith.

Reports differ on the year he died. He was among the last living men who had stood at 'Aqaba.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih Muslim, Book of Hajj, narrated by Jabir ibn Abdullah — his account of the Farewell Hajj
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley — the flood, the unchanged bodies at forty-six years, and the reburial after six months, narrated from Jabir through Abu Nadra and Ata'; Sahih Muslim, Book of Hajj; al-Bukhari, Sahih, Book of Knowledge, chapter on travelling in search of knowledge

quiz.prompt: What position did Jabir's father hold among the Ansar at the second pledge of 'Aqaba?

options.text: He was the reciter sent ahead to Madinah
He was one of the twelve leaders chosen from the seventy
He was the treasurer of Banu Salama
He carried the banner of al-Khazraj

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Jabir was at 'Aqaba as a boy, standing among the seventy while his father guaranteed the pledge on behalf of a clan that had to live with the consequences.

quiz.prompt: Why was Jabir absent from Badr and Uhud?

options.text: He was ill both times
He was sent to Makkah on an errand
His father held him back to look after his sisters
He was judged too young by the Prophet ﷺ

quiz.citation: Sahih Muslim, Book of Jihad and Expeditions, narrated by Jabir ibn Abdullah
quiz.scholar_reflection: He said he went on nineteen expeditions in all, and that the two most famous were not among them. After Uhud he never missed one.

quiz.prompt: Why did Jabir marry a woman who had been married before rather than a young girl?

options.text: His father had arranged the match before Uhud
He wanted someone who could comb his sisters' hair and manage them
He could not afford the dowry of a virgin
The Prophet ﷺ instructed him to

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Marriage, narrated by Jabir ibn Abdullah
quiz.scholar_reflection: He was asked one question on a road home from a campaign and volunteered the whole calculation. The sisters came before his own preference.

quiz.prompt: When Jabir pulled the cloth from his dead father's face and wept, what happened?

options.text: The Prophet ﷺ told him to stop, as the others did
The Companions tried to stop him; the Prophet ﷺ did not, and spoke of angels shading his father
He was removed from the field
The Prophet ﷺ ordered a second shroud brought

quiz.citation: Narrated from Jabir ibn Abdullah through Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Weep for him or do not weep. The choice was handed back to the boy, and the news about the angels was given to him either way.

quiz.prompt: Why did the Prophet ﷺ order Abdullah ibn Amr and Amr ibn al-Jamuh buried in one grave?

options.text: There was no time to dig two
They were brothers
Because of the love and close friendship between them in this world
They had died at the same moment

quiz.citation: Reported from Malik ibn Anas — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: The instruction was given with its reason attached: bury these two who loved one another in this world in one grave. One was tall and one was short, and they were recognised by that.

quiz.prompt: Jabir's Islam began with a night pledge and then years of being told he was needed at home. How do you handle being given the unglamorous assignment?

options.text: Badly — I want to be where the important thing is happening
I take it and resent it quietly
I have come to prefer it, and I am not sure that is humility
I take it if someone I respect explains why

quiz.citation: Sahih Muslim, Book of Jihad and Expeditions, narrated by Jabir ibn Abdullah
quiz.scholar_reflection: He missed Badr and Uhud and became one of the great teachers of the ummah anyway. The two facts are connected, not opposed.

quiz.prompt: He asked the Prophet ﷺ to come with him so the creditors would not be excessive. What do you do when you are in debt to people who have a right to press you?

options.text: I avoid them until it becomes an emergency
I go to them first, before they come to me
I bring someone with me because I cannot face it alone
I have never been in real debt and I do not know

quiz.citation: Narrated from Jabir ibn Abdullah through Amir ash-Sha'bi — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He did not ask for the debt to be cancelled or paid for him. He asked for company while it was settled honestly.

quiz.prompt: Six months after the burial he moved a stranger out of his father's grave because he could not rest. What unfinished thing keeps returning to you?

options.text: Something about a death I did not handle the way I wanted to
A conversation I never had with someone still alive
Nothing — I close things and move on
Too many things to name one

quiz.citation: Narrated from Jabir ibn Abdullah through Abu Nadra — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He is one of the great jurists of Madinah and he still went back and reopened a grave over a feeling. Grief does not defer to rank.

quiz.prompt: He rode a month to Syria to hear one hadith from one man. What is the furthest you have gone for something you could not get where you were?

options.text: Nowhere — I take what is available locally
Some distance, and it changed how I understood it
I go far for work and never for this
I keep planning the journey and not making it

quiz.citation: al-Bukhari, Sahih, Book of Knowledge, chapter on travelling in search of knowledge
quiz.scholar_reflection: One hadith. A month each way. He was already a man people travelled to see.

quiz.prompt: His father's last instruction was about his daughters, not about the battle. What would your last instruction be about?
quiz.slider_label: What you would leave word about

options.text: The people I have been carrying
My debts and what I have left unsettled
Something I want understood correctly about me
I have honestly never thought it through

quiz.citation: Narrated from Jabir ibn Abdullah through Abu Nadra — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He said he hoped to be among the first struck the next day, and in the same breath gave instructions about the girls. He had ordered his priorities before the night ended.
